title: Tanker Hit Near Khasab as Hormuz Traffic Stays About 65% Below Pre-War Levels
excerpt: UKMTO reported a fresh projectile strike on an outbound tanker on Saturday, six tanker attacks in a week, and oil flows down to about 10 million barrels a day — with Indian crew among the week's casualties.
body:
• A tanker sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz was hit on its stern by an unidentified projectile about 11 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab on Saturday, UKMTO said — no injuries were reported and the environmental impact is unknown.
  • UKMTO's weekly overview counted 263 transits in the seven days to November 18, down from 308 a week earlier, with traffic about 65% below pre-conflict levels; six tankers were attacked during the week.
  • Oil flows through the strait fell to about 10 million barrels a day by November 10, down from 13.4 million at the start of the month, according to Kpler tracking data cited by Bloomberg.
  • For Gulf-based readers and anyone with family working at sea: UKMTO has recorded 106 incidents in the strait since February 28, and the Joint Maritime Information Center assesses the threat level as severe.

Another tanker has been hit in the Strait of Hormuz. A vessel sailing outbound through the strait was struck on its stern by an unidentified projectile about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, on Oman's Musandam Peninsula, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Saturday. No injuries were reported, and the environmental impact of the incident was unknown, Reuters reported. Khasab sits at the entrance to the strait, a waterway that carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil supplies before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran began.

"Energy carriers made up half of all transits, according to US Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping figures cited in the overview."

Traffic is falling, attacks are not

The Saturday strike capped the heaviest recent week in the strait. UKMTO's weekly security overview, released November 20, counted 263 vessel transits in the seven days to November 18 — 148 inbound and 115 outbound — down from 308 the previous week, leaving traffic about 65% below pre-conflict levels, Marine Insight reported. Energy carriers made up half of all transits, according to US Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping figures cited in the overview. UKMTO reported attacks on six tankers during the week — four in the strait and two in the Persian Gulf. Two of the attacked tankers needed assistance, none was reported sunk, and the agency noted it publishes only incidents verified through primary sources while knowing of more it cannot independently verify.

The week's casualties included Indian seafarers. On November 17 a tanker hit about 13 nautical miles north of Khasab caught fire; the shipping company confirmed one crew member missing and 11 injured. An LPG tanker attacked on November 16 was struck again on November 17, caught fire in its engine room and was abandoned by its crew — India's Ministry of External Affairs reported one of its crew members missing and two injured. UKMTO has now recorded 106 incidents in the strait since the conflict began on February 28, and the Joint Maritime Information Center assesses the threat level as severe, meaning an attack is highly likely.

The oil flow underneath

The shipping squeeze is showing up in the cargo numbers. Oil flows through Hormuz fell to approximately 10 million barrels a day by November 10, down from 13.4 million barrels a day at the start of the month, according to Kpler tracking data cited by Bloomberg on November 19, with very large crude carrier loadings from the Middle East Gulf down to 7.4 million barrels a day in the first half of November from 9.3 million across October. Shipping through the strait has been disrupted since Iran moved to close the waterway after the conflict erupted on February 28, Reuters noted, and the November pattern — roughly one attack a day through the first 19 days of the month, per UKMTO data cited by Bloomberg — is pushing more owners to weigh the route against the risk.

What to watch

There is no sign in the latest reporting of the strait reopening to normal traffic. For the diaspora, the exposure is direct: Indian crew sail many of the tankers transiting the Gulf, Gulf-based families depend on ports whose traffic is running at about a third of pre-war levels, and every sustained fall in Hormuz flows feeds the fuel and freight prices readers pay elsewhere. The next UKMTO weekly overview will show whether the November 20–21 strikes near Khasab mark a new tempo or the peak of the current one.
